name: journal-who-was-lying-at-antioch.json
content:
In the early church two of its best minds argued over whether Paul told the truth about Antioch. Jerome said the quarrel with Peter was staged. Augustine said that made Paul a liar, and worse. Both men are on record, and the church never settled which of them was right.

Two readings in the church

Paul writes that he opposed Peter "to his face, because he stood condemned", and told him before everyone that he was forcing Gentiles to live like Jews.1 Early readers found this hard to accept. Peter was the first of the apostles, and Paul charges him with hypocrisy.

Jerome, in his commentary on Galatians, followed Origen: the quarrel was an arrangement between the two apostles, staged to teach the Gentiles without shaming Peter before the Jews. Augustine disagreed. He wrote to Jerome more than once, and he returned to the question in a treatise On Lying.

What Augustine wrote

The treatise dates from about 395. Its last section answers the defenders of Peter directly.

The reasoning is short. If Paul only pretended to rebuke Peter, then Paul lied in a letter written for the doctrine of piety. Worse, he lied after swearing a few verses earlier: "In what I am writing to you, before God, I do not lie!"3 Augustine calls that perjury.

Years later he put the same view to Jerome. Peter "fell into the fault of pretending to yield concurrence", he wrote, and for that reason "Paul wrote most truly of him, that he saw him not walking uprightly, according to the truth of the gospel".4

What Augustine concedes

Augustine gives Peter up. His own words say that Peter had fallen into a "pravity of way", a crooked way of living. The strongest defender of Paul's honesty in the early church therefore agrees that the leader of the apostles was in the wrong at Antioch.

He pays for Paul's honesty with Peter's.

What a study Bible admits

A modern study Bible reads the passage as Paul's reply to critics. Its note on Galatians 2:11 to 14 begins:

The note goes on to say that the Gentiles are the people meant, and that Paul tells the story of Peter to answer the charge. The note confirms that the charge was made, and that Galatians is the answer to it.

The oath

Paul puts his word under oath before he tells the story. That is why Jerome's reading is costly. If the report of Antioch is true, Peter erred. If it is a staged scene, Paul swore falsely.

Each choice costs the church one of its apostles.

A Muslim reading

In the Islamic account ʿĪsā and his disciples lived by the law of Mūsā. Seen that way, Peter's withdrawal from the Gentile table is loyalty to the law, and the man who calls it hypocrisy is the one who never met ʿĪsā. See [paulus_link slug="the-parting-with-barnabas"]the parting with Barnabas[/paulus_link].

The verdict

Jerome saved Peter by giving up Paul's word. Augustine saved Paul's word by giving up Peter's conduct. A reader who wants both apostles to have been truthful and right has no reading left.

Antioch and the charge of lying: questions readers ask

What did Augustine say about Paul and Peter at Antioch?

That Paul told the truth and Peter was at fault. In On Lying 43 he argues that calling the quarrel a pretence makes Paul a liar and a perjurer.

Did Jerome think the quarrel was staged?

Yes. In his commentary on Galatians he followed Origen and read it as an arrangement between Peter and Paul.

Where does Paul swear that he does not lie?

In Galatians 1:20, shortly before the Antioch story: "In what I am writing to you, before God, I do not lie!"

  2. Augustine, On Lying (De mendacio) 43, trans. H. Browne, in Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series, vol. 3, ed. Philip Schaff (Buffalo, NY: Christian Literature Publishing, 1887). ↩
  3. Galatians 1:20 (ESV). ↩
  4. Augustine, Letter 82 (to Jerome) 15, trans. J. G. Cunningham, in Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series, vol. 1, ed. Philip Schaff (Buffalo, NY: Christian Literature Publishing, 1887). ↩
  5. Faithlife Study Bible (Bellingham, WA: Logos Bible Software, 2012), note on Galatians 2:11 to 14. ↩
